Items.Authors: Jasmina Lazendic-Galloway, Maria Rita Eusébio Vale Lima, Jan Geralt bij de Vaate, Raj Rajan, Pietro Zucca, Mark Bentum, Peter Roelfsema, Wouter Laauwen, Antonio Vecchio, Christiaan Brinkering
Items.Title: L‑FIRE: A space‑based interferometric array for low‑frequency (1–40 MHz) radio astronomy
Items.Abstract: L-FIRE (Low-Frequency Interferometric Radio Explorer) is a mission concept for a spaceborne low-frequency radio interferometer operating from 1–40 MHz, a regime inaccessible from the ground. A scalable cluster of free-flying spacecraft forms a long-baseline distributed aperture using orthogonal dipole antennas and onboard correlation. The design addresses key challenges in antenna performance, formation flying, calibration, RFI mitigation, and high-volume data processing, while enabling future growth to larger constellations. L-FIRE will open a new observational window for heliospheric physics, star–planet interactions, and Galactic studies, and will deliver the first comprehensive sky survey at ultra-low radio frequencies.

Items.Authors: R. Lynne Jones, Peter Yoachim, Eric H. Neilsen, Tiago Ribeiro, Erik Dennihy, Sean MacBride
Items.Title: Scheduling the LSST: commissioning the Rubin Feature Based Scheduler
Items.Abstract: Rubin Observatory will acquire about two million science observations during the course of the ten year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). Planning these observations is the work of the Rubin Feature Based Scheduler (FBS), every 30 seconds, every twilight to twilight. The FBS has been generating simulated observations for over ten years, driving the development and co-optimization the LSST survey strategy and FBS algorithms, in a collaborative process between the project and the astronomical community under the guidance of the LSST Survey Cadence Optimization Committee (SCOC). The FBS has been in active use with the Rubin Auxiliary Telescope for several years building the framework for interactions between the FBS and summit system. The commissioning of LSSTCam in 2025 marked the first on-sky use of the FBS with the Simonyi Telescope, with an FBS configuration representative of the full LSST. We report on successes and lessons learned.

Items.Authors: Gregory J. Fetzer, Steven E. Rako, Nathan Woody, Katie Baldwin, Philip Hinz, Daren Dillon, Jeffery Roark, Elinor Gates, Juan Chilla, Celine D'Orgeville, Noelia Martinez Rey, Robert Johnson
Items.Title: On-sky demonstration of a semiconductor VECSEL-based sodium guide-star system
Items.Abstract: This presentation will address a semiconductor laser sodium guidestar system operated on sky from the Lick Observatory Shane Telescope. The speaker will discuss design, laboratory performance measurements, telescope installation (September of 2025) and subsequent operation with Shane Telescope AO systems. The system has been operated to support both system performance analysis and astronomical observations for many months.

Items.Authors: Haoran Kang, Takafumi Kojima, Takeshi Sakai, Yoichi Tamura, Shun Ishii, Akio Taniguchi, Masato Hagimoto, Masato Kato, Taku Nakajima, Tai Oshima, Sho Masui, Issei Watanabe
Items.Title: A wideband 210-350 GHz millimeter-wave receiver for LMT-FINER
Items.Abstract: The FINER project is developing two wideband dual-polarization sideband-separating receivers covering 120–210 GHz and 210–350 GHz to efficiently identify high-redshift galaxy candidates in the early universe. Based on high-Jc SIS mixer technology originally developed for the ALMA WSU, the FINER receivers are designed to provide an IF bandwidth of 3–21 GHz per sideband and per polarization, approximately five times wider than the current ALMA specifications. After installation on the LMT, these receivers are expected to offer highly efficient spectral-scanning capability among (sub)millimeter-wave facilities in the northern-hemisphere. This paper reports the initial laboratory characterization of the 210–350 GHz receiver. The measured single-sideband receiver noise temperature is approximately 100 K over most of the RF band. Digital sideband separation was also demonstrated using a wideband spectrometer array, achieving an image rejection ratio of around 20 dB in the initial tests.

Items.Authors: Shaojie Chen, Suresh Sivanandam, Olivier Lardière, Gavin Hay, Sarik Jeram, Béatrice Lessard-Hamel, Denis Brousseau, Simon Thibault, Jenny Atwood, Mark Barnet, Jiayi, Emma Xu, Saugata Dutt, Scott Christie
Items.Title: Final optical design and performance assessment of a multi-object adaptive optics-fed infrared integral-field spectrograph (GIRMOS)
Items.Abstract: We present the final end-to-end optical design of GIRMOS developed to take advantage of the adaptive optics corrected field at the Gemini North telescope. GIRMOS consists of object selection pick-offs, multi-object adaptive optics, and four identical Integral-Field Spectrographs (IFSes), which employ image slicers to arrange the integral field along a slit. The analysis shows the expected performance meets the scientific requirements and the design comply with manufacturability requirements. This paper summarizes the final optical design, engineering validation of critical components, and system performance assessment by using Structural–Thermal–Optical Performance (STOP) analysis. The results presented in this work demonstrate that GIRMOS optical design has reached a mature engineering stage and provides a solid foundation for instrument production.

Items.Authors: Michael Goodwin, Jon Lawrence, Tiger Wang, Summer Luo, Dani Guzman, Timothy Chin, Jessica Zheng, Helen McGregor, Lew Waller, Tony Farrell, Zhemin Cai, Ali Ghari Zadeh, Jon Moller, Christopher Coote, Jake Linden, Dylan Simpfendorfer, Max Hewletta, Andrew Rakich, Thierry Fusco, Delphine Barbon-Dubosc, Carlos Correia, Benoit Neichel, Pierre Jouve, Arnaud Striffling, Julien Charton, Julie Magri, Anne-Sophie Bruni Favier
Items.Title: Model-based systems engineering progress for the Gemini North Adaptive Optics Bench in critical design phase
Items.Abstract: The Gemini North Adaptive Optics Bench is a key opto-mechanical subsystem of the Gemini North Adaptive Optics facility and has completed Critical Design Review (CDR), positioning it to enter the Build Phase. This paper reports the systems engineering progress that enabled CDR success, emphasising requirements decomposition and traceability, interface management across a geographically distributed consortium, and maturation of verification and validation planning. Central to the approach is a SysML-based Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) implementation in which the system model is the authoritative source for requirements, operational concepts, architecture, and interface definition. This model-centric workflow has strengthened requirement-to-architecture traceability, supported consistent interface documentation, and improved visibility of integration and compliance risks. We conclude with the verification strategy, remaining activities, and lessons learned from applying MBSE.

Items.Authors: David Le Mignant, Coralie Neiner, Jean-Claude Bouret, Luca Fossati, Pollux Consortium
Items.Title: Pollux: high-resolution precision spectroscopy and polarimetry for the Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: Pollux is a proposed high-resolution spectrograph (R>75,000–100,000) with polarimetry capabilities for NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory, covering 100–1888 nm across five echelle spectrographs. It enables simultaneous spectroscopy and polarimetry (Stokes I, Q, U, V), addressing key science: exoplanet atmospheres, star-planet interactions, galactic evolution, and cosmic magnetic fields.   Pollux aligns with HWO’s goals, supporting studies of habitable worlds, stellar magnetism, and intergalactic media. Its design includes UV/NIR polarimeters, advanced gratings, and space-qualified detectors. This paper presents Pollux’s science objectives, instrument architecture, and development roadmap, highlighting its potential as a transformative tool for astrophysics.

Items.Authors: Alessandro Costa, Emilio Mastriani, Federico Incardona, Kevin Munari, Sebastiano Spinello, Fulvio Gianotti, Ismam Abu
Items.Title: ServiMon: AI-enabled performance prediction for astronomical SCADA infrastructures
Items.Abstract: ServiMon, as an AI-Enabled Performance Prediction for Astronomical SCADA Infrastructure, presents a framework designed to anticipate performance variability and software inefficiencies within observatory control environments.  Building on aggregated behavioral and performance data from the CTAO ACADA software stack, ServiMon integrates machine-learning and time-series segmentation techniques to detect anomalous patterns, forecast performance degradation, and support more informed maintenance strategies.  In contrast to approaches centered on physical sensor telemetry, the study focuses on software-level indicators—latency, throughput, resource utilization, and service stability—captured across the distributed SCADA ecosystem.  The preliminary results discussed here demonstrate the potential of ServiMon to deliver early predictive insights and to enhance the operational robustness of complex astronomical infrastructures.

Items.Authors: Florence Laurent, Johan Richard, Rémi Giroud, Davor Krajnovic, Alexandre Jeanneau, Manuel Adler Abreu, Angela Adamo, Théo Battrel, Didier Boudon, Zhemin Cai, Diane Chapuis Kerouanton, Christopher Coote, Malak Galal, Joshua J. Guy, Robert J. Harris, Andreas Kelz, Audrey Lanotte, Jonathon Lawrence, Rémy Le Breton, Helen McGregor, Gloria Mellinand, Jonathan Moller, Manuel Monteiro, Giuliano Parma, Arlette Pecontal-Rousset, Peter M. Weilbacher
Items.Title: ESO-VLT BlueMuse Instrument - conceptual design for phase A
Items.Abstract: BlueMUSE is a blue-optimised, medium-resolution panoramic integral-field spectrograph being developed for the VLT and now entering its construction phase. Designed for high transmission down to 350 nm, with an average spectral resolution of R~3500 and a 1 arcmin² field of view, it will enable a wide range of new galactic and extragalactic science applications. The instrument is composed of several subsystems aligned along the light path: a calibration unit that replicates VLT optical conditions, fore-optics that reshape the focal image, and splitting and relay optics that divide the field into 16 channels. Each channel feeds an integral field unit housing an image slicer, spectrograph, and detector vessel with a 4k×4k CCD. The system includes vacuum and cryogenic cooling, data-reduction software for producing data cubes, and a main structure enclosed in a passive thermal housing. This paper outlines the Phase A baseline architecture, interfaces, and global concepts.

Items.Authors: Jyotirmay Paul, Stefan Kraus, Michael Ireland, Daniel Lancaster, Sorabh Chhabra, Narsireddy Anugu, Owain Snaith
Items.Title: Design and development of longitudinal atmospheric dispersion corrector for BIFROST/Asgard
Items.Abstract: The ASGARD suite includes BIFROST, which is designed to enhance VLTI interferometry capabilities. BIFROST opens new spectral windows in the Y, J, and H bands, enabling fringe tracking on bright on-axis stars while observing faint off-axis sources. Its pre-injection unit incorporates a Longitudinal Dispersion Corrector (LDC) and a lithium niobate plate, followed by a fibre-injection module feeding an all-in-one beam combiner. The LDC compensates for differential atmospheric dispersion between telescopes, preserving fringe contrast across wide spectral bands and ensuring efficient fibre coupling.   Laboratory calibration demonstrates precise fringe alignment, stable fibre injection, and minimal residual dispersion. We present both laboratory and on-sky calibration results, confirming the readiness of BIFROST for high-precision, wide-band interferometric observations.

Items.Authors: Jingwei Hu, Mo Zhang, Yuan Liu, Chichuan Jin, Weimin Yuan
Items.Title: Design and optimization of observation scheduling for the Einstein Probe mission
Items.Abstract: The Einstein Probe (EP) is a wide-field X-ray mission launched in January 2024 to monitor the dynamic high-energy universe and discover transient and variable sources. Efficient observation scheduling is essential for maximizing its scientific return. This presentation introduces the design principles and optimization strategies of the EP observation scheduling system, which supports routine survey observations, Target-of-Opportunity (ToO) observations, and multi-messenger follow-up campaigns. We highlight the core scheduling logic, priority framework, automated decision-making pipeline, and the operational workflow that enables EP to balance long-term survey goals with rapid responses to transient alerts. Early in-orbit performance and examples of scheduling outcomes are also discussed.

Items.Authors: Shun Yoneda, Takeo Minezaki
Items.Title: Development of a Rayleigh laser guide star system using a SPAD-based wavefront sensor with built-in range-gating
Items.Abstract: We are developing a Rayleigh Laser Guide Star (RGS) system for adaptive optics (AO) utilizing a Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) image sensor. SPAD image sensors offer nanosecond-precision electronic gating, enabling the Wavefront Sensor (WFS) to isolate backscattered light from specific altitudes without requiring external shutter mechanisms such as Pockels cells, thereby simplifying the RGS system and facilitating WFS miniaturization. We successfully demonstrated range-gated imaging in a ground experiment over a 50-meter distance, achieving an extinction ratio of approximately 70,000, which satisfies the requirements for practical RGS operation. Furthermore, on-sky experiments with natural stars confirmed the sensor's design sensitivity and demonstrated WFS operation at 900 Hz, fast enough for AO wavefront sensing. Future work involves extending the ground experiment to 500 meters and conducting on-sky RGS experiments.

Items.Authors: Andrew Chael
Items.Title: Dynamic magnetic fields around black holes revealed by the Event Horizon Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) is a network of millimeter-wavelength radio telescopes that spans the globe from Greenland to the South Pole. Using Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI), the EHT has repeatedly imaged two supermassive black holes on event horizon scales, in the giant elliptical galaxy (M87*) and in the Milky Way’s Galactic Center (Sgr A*).  In this talk, I will discuss what recent EHT observations of these two paradigmatic sources have taught us about the dynamical environments close to these black holes that span three orders of magnitude in black hole mass. I will also discuss how future advances in both EHT observations and theoretical simulations will better constrain the dynamical near-horizon environment and illuminate the connection between supermassive black holes and extragalactic jets at the launching point.

Items.Authors: Asier Larringan, Amaia Ormaetxe, Gaizka Murga, Paul Jolley, Steffan Lewis
Items.Title: The acceptance of the Extremely Large Telescope Prefocal Stations Main System
Items.Abstract: Located on the Nasmyth Platforms A and B, the Prefocal Stations of the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) constitute the final opto-mechanical elements before the light from the telescope reaches its focus. Both units alternately distribute the light collected by the telescope’s giant optical system to the science instruments and other test equipment, and they deliver focal-plane and pupil images of three natural guide stars. They also provide the optical sensing required to support the phasing of the ELT primary mirrors, as well as diagnostics and optical maintenance.    The acceptance of the so-called PFS Main System, supplied by IDOM, has been achieved after the successful completion of the Factory Assembly and Testing in Bilbao. The equipment is now ready for integration into the ELT; however, while construction of the telescope progresses, it will remain in Bilbao for an ESO testing phase and will subsequently be shipped to Chile for a temporary storage period prior to its installation

Items.Authors: Frédéric Zamkotsian, Simon Ans, Guillaume Demesy, Patrick Lanzoni, Quentin Tanguy, Andrei Mursa, Roland Salut, Nicolas Passilly, Cindy Bellanger, Jérôme Primot
Items.Title: Metasurfaces for high-contrast imaging and spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: We are developing at LAM new instrument concepts using breakthrough technologies, including micro-mirrors arrays, non-planar blazed gratings and metasurfaces, for next generation spectro-imagers and coronographs. Design, modelling, realization and characterization of nanostructured blazed gratings and scalar vortex coronograph for high-contrast imaging are under way.

Items.Authors: Annemieke W. Janssen, Gabby Aitink-Kroes, Ester Aranzana, Andrey Baryshev, Christiaan Brinkerink, Alexey Grishaev, Piet Holbrouck, Michael Janssen, Julian van den Noort
Items.Title: Africa Millimetre Telescope: front-end design
Items.Abstract: The Africa Millimetre Telescope (AMT) will be a sub-millimetre radio telescope in Namibia, observing in the frequency range 35 - 373 GHz. It can both observe as single dish, and as part of Very Large Baseline Interferometers, like the Event Horizon Telescope. At a minimum, the ALMA bands 1,2, 6 and 7 are part of the design. Potential extensions include adding a low-frequeny section (8-22 GHz). The paper describes the preliminary design of the AMT front-end, which includes optics in the cabin, and the cryostat with receivers. The requirement to simultaneously observe band 1 and 2, as well as band 2,6 and 7, makes it a unique and complex optical design, consisting of three dichroics, and a challenging alignment strategy.

Items.Authors: David Brodrick, Valentina Viotto, Anthony Horton, Pierre Haguenauer, Tristan Monnier, Hana Benhizia, Luca Marafatto, Dionne Haynes, Gaston Gausachs, Ulf Seemann, Roger Haynes, Jennifer Burgess, Trevor Mendel, Francois Rigaut
Items.Title: MAVIS: a model-based verification framework for distributed integration
Items.Abstract: MAVIS is a complex astronomical instrument whose Manufacturing, Assembly, Integration, and Test (MAIT) activities are distributed across multiple Consortium institutes, with final re-integration and commissioning at ESO’s Paranal Observatory. To support this distributed MAIT programme, the Consortium has adopted a model-based verification framework linking requirements, verification activities, and system integration state.    Initial verification is performed progressively at each Consortium node, with verification results forming mandatory input to Local Acceptance Reviews prior to shipment. As integration advances, additional verification activities become possible. Central to this approach is the definition of System Configuration Levels (SCLs), representing discrete integration states. Requirements and verification activities are managed in a shared SysML model using TestCase elements linked to requirements, enabling traceability and coordinated verification across the Consortium.

Items.Authors: Marie Larrieu, Daniel Lecron, Alexandre Tzeou Hah Fauline, Frédéric Panzano, Kacem El Hadi, Sebastiano Ligori, Vito Capobianco, Maria Isabel Carnerero, Olivier Boebion, Yan Caujolle, Adrien Malgoyre, Thomas Fenouillet, Paul Bohard, Francisco-José Antunes, Jean-Philippe Rutault, Elodie Bourrec, Thierry Contini, Hermine Schnetler, Roser Pello
Items.Title: MOSAIC at ELT: a first step towards an instrument control deployment over Europe
Items.Abstract: Testing an astrophysical instrument before it is installed at the telescope requires an interaction between the control part of the instrument (graphical user interfaces, control software, control hardware), and its electro-opto-mechanical elements (detectors, motors, sensors, lamps). Usually, this final validation is carried in a single integration site. Due to its size, MOSAIC may not be tested in a single European site. This paper presents some tests carried between European sites to validate the concept of a distributed deployment of an instrument control architecture based on the ESO ELT control Framework.

Items.Authors: Jesper M. Skottfelt, Martin Barstow, Joanna Barstow, Francis Bell, Oliver Blake, Becky Canning, Dan Dicken, James Doherty, Christophe Dumas, Paul Eccleston, Sandy Fok, Eduardo Gonzalez-Solares, William Grainger, Or Graur, Anna Maskolenko, Sean McGee, Cassandra Mercury, Chris Miller, Christopher Pattison, Michael Plissi, Richard Robinson, Piyal Samara-Ratna, Bhargav N. Swamy, David D. Walker, Nicholas Walton, Samatha Youles
Items.Title: Study of a Four-Band Far-UV to Near-IR High-Resolution Imager for the Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) is NASA’s planned flagship mission to detect and characterise Earth-like exoplanets around nearby Sun-like stars. A UK Space Agency–funded feasibility study has investigated a high-resolution imager (HRI) as a potential UK-led contribution. Science requirements drove performance across the 90–2500 nm range, including support for sub-microarcsec astrometry for exo-Earth mass measurements and observatory guiding.  The study evaluated instrument architectures, optical designs, detector technologies, and system constraints, resulting in a four-channel concept covering the Far-UV, Near-UV, Visible, and Near-IR, with simultaneous imaging in selected bands. We present performance, mass, power, and thermal analyses, identify key technology challenges, and outline future development plans. The results demonstrate the scientific and technical feasibility of a UK-led HRI for HWO and strong alignment with UK industrial and academic expertise.

Items.Authors: Gary J. Hill, Hanshin Lee, John M. Good, Casey Kyte, Jason G. Vestuto, Joshua Oppor, Brian L. Vattiat, Niv Drory, Gregory R. Zeimann, Michael P. Smith, Joseph R. Tufts, Greg Bredthauer, Briana L Indahl, Christian Haubitz-Reinke, Ripley C. Gregg
Items.Title: VIRUS2: first deployment of a next generation replicated integral field spectrograph with wide field and broad wavelength coverage
Items.Abstract: VIRUS2 is a new NSF-funded fiber-fed multiplexed integral field spectrograph consisting of 6 units, each with 4 spectral channels, providing large on-sky area coverage coupled with broad spectral coverage (370-930 nm at R~2000). On the McDonald Observatory 2.7 m Harlan J Smith Telescope, VIRUS2 covers a 1.7 by 1.3 = 2.3 sq. arcmin. field of view, with full fill-factor. VIRUS2 employs a novel beam-switch module (BSM) within the fiber feed to split the light into the 4 spectral channels. The design of VIRUS2 emphasizes stability and careful calibration, with scrambling in the BSM, compact spectrograph format, and tight thermal control.     Science drivers for VIRUS2 are resolved studies of nearby galaxies, their circum-galactic environments, and their dark matter content, blind spectroscopic surveys and transients. We provide an overview of the instrument and describe the assembly and present results from the first phase of commissioning.

Items.Authors: Martin Steglich, Michael Helgert, Gabor Matthäus, Matthias Burkhardt, Alexander Kalies, Carsten Stock
Items.Title: Holographic low straylight gratings for astronomical applications
Items.Abstract: For about 20 years ZEISS Microoptics is involved in the design, manufacturing and characterization of holographic, low stray light, high efficiency gratings for space & science applications. Various ESA and NASA missions have been launched or are in flight preparation with spectrometers equipped with gratings from ZEISS. In addition, we routinely customize gratings for further science customers, from Soft-X-ray beamline to IR spectroscopy, covering flat and imaging, as well as freeform surface figures or grisms. This talk comprehensively demonstrates ZEISS’ capabilities for the manufacturing of holographic, customized science gratings, and highlights a selection of past science grating projects.

Items.Authors: Andrea Bianco, Michele Frangiamore, Andrea Tozzi, Anna Brucalassi, Kjetil Dohlen, Will Saunders, Alexandre Jeanneau, Corentin Cudennec, David Lee
Items.Title: WST, the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope: dispersing elements
Items.Abstract: The Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST) is a planned 12-meter-class dedicated spectroscopic facility designed to address key scientific challenges through large spectroscopic surveys. This paper presents the current status of Work Package 4.7 and in particular to the design and challenges of the dispersing elements required for the three kinds of instruments; namely, Low resolution, high resolution and integral field spectrographs. It is fundamental to pave to way to technologies that secure the grating procurement.  Different approaches and optimization routes are selected for the low and high resolution systems. Main challenges will be described and possible solutions proposed related to the actual and future TRL

Items.Authors: Benoît Neichel, Darío G. Pérez, Esteban Vera Rojas, Guillaume Bourdarot, Vincent Chambouleyron, Cedric Heritier, Thierry Fusco, Nicolas Vedrenne, Frank Eisenhauer
Items.Title: Towards an extended VLTI: turbulence characterization for kilometer-scale optical links at Paranal
Items.Abstract: Future VLTI extensions aim for kilometer-scale baselines to reach tens of micro-arcsecond resolution. A first step is to connect a new telescope on the VISTA platform to the VLTI, creating a 1.4 km baseline using free-space optical transmission, though the turbulence along this horizontal path remains unknown. We propose a dedicated experiment using two small telescopes facing each other across the link, combining a wide-field Shack–Hartmann sensor for turbulence tomography with an event-based camera to capture fast, anisotropic effects. Built in early 2026 with tests starting mid-2026, this will provide the first long-term characterization of kilometer-scale horizontal turbulence at Paranal and key inputs for future FSO systems and extended VLTI baselines.

Items.Authors: Ferdinando Patat
Items.Title: A genetic algorithm for peer-review panel composition
Items.Abstract: This paper presents a genetic algorithm designed to optimize the composition of classical peer-review panels in large proposal-handling systems. Although developed for ESO, the method is general and applicable to any facility using category-based review panels. The algorithm represents each panel configuration as a chromosome and evolves populations of candidate solutions through mutation, crossover, and selection, while enforcing strict constraints such as fixed panel sizes and immovable panel chairs. Panel quality is assessed through a multi-component fitness function that measures imbalances in expertise, gender, geographic distribution, and seniority. Each component is normalized using ranges derived from large randomized populations. Tests on real reviewer data demonstrate that the algorithm rapidly converges toward balanced panel configurations and naturally produces a ranked set of near-optimal solutions that allows additional practical constraints to be applied.

Items.Authors: Johnny Esteves de Queiroz, Christopher W. Stubbs, Elana Urbach, Paulina Venegas Salas, Petr Kubánek, Brian Stalder
Items.Title: Forecast for dome thermal control: a hybrid deep learning framework for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory
Items.Abstract: Precise thermal control is a prerequisite for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory to meet the image-quality requirements of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). Temperature gradients between the dome air, the primary/tertiary mirror (M1M3), and the ambient environment drive both dome and mirror seeing. The observatory employs a dome HVAC system and a forced-air system behind the M1M3 mirror. To optimize these, we present NBEATSx+Ridge, a two-stage causal architecture predicting twilight temperatures using only historical local weather data. Evaluated on 2025 data, it spans the distinct horizons of both systems. For long-term dome conditioning, it delivers stable morning targets refined to within $1^{\circ}\text{C}$ of twilight by midday. For the M1M3 mirror, short-term forecasts achieve an RMSE of $0.80^{\circ}\text{C}$, meaning predictive errors no longer limit performance—the system is bounded only by the mirror’s $0.7^{\circ}\text{C}/\text{hr}$ cooling limit, ensuring full thermal.

Items.Authors: Julien Drevon, Ferreol Soulez, Joel Sanchez-Bermudez, Jens Kammerer, Gioia Rau
Items.Title: Optical interferometry imaging contest XI
Items.Abstract: Over the past decades, image reconstruction in optical interferometry has become a key tool for astrophysical research, driven by major advances with instruments such as MATISSE and GRAVITY at the VLTI, and the very new GPAO+ upgrade. Since 2004, the biennial “Interferometric Imaging Contest” helps the community to provide a clear view on our capability to reconstruct astrophysical environments using interferometric data. In 2025, we celebrate the XIth edition of this initiative, continuing to provide an open platform for researchers to present their latest developments, benchmark reconstruction techniques, and explore future directions for high-resolution interferometric imaging.

Items.Authors: Aglaé Kellerer, Henri Bonnet, Michael Esselborn, Pierre Haguenauer, Johannes Kolmeder, Nicholas C. Kornweibel, Oliver Pfuhl, Christophe Vérinaud, Julien Woillez, Martin Dimmler, Emanuela Ciattaglia, Byron Engler, Andreas Reinacher, Jason Spyromilio
Items.Title: Wavefront control on the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT)
Items.Abstract: The ELT will undergo a sequence of wavefront-control activities before first light and also during operations. Achieving diffraction-limited performance requires precise mirror alignment, accurate phasing of the segmented primary mirror, and correction of pupil fragmentation caused by the telescope spiders. This contribution outlines the ELT Wavefront Control Group’s strategy to reach this state on-axis, using wavefront sensors in the Phasing and Diagnostic Station (PDS) and the Pre-Focal Station (PFS), together with distributed actuators that position and shape the mirrors. We describe the planned sequence -- from segment capture and coherencing to phasing of the 798-segment primary mirror -- and the subsequent closure of the single-conjugate adaptive-optics loop.

Items.Authors: Shaolin Xiong
Items.Title: GECAM mission: a constellation of full-sky gamma-ray monitors in multi-messenger multi-wavelength era
Items.Abstract: Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is a constellation composed of four all-sky x-ray/gamma-ray monitors (GECAM-A/B/C/D) on different spacecrafts, dedicated to observe high energy transients, including GRBs (especially those associated with GW and HEN) and SGRs (especially those associated with FRB). Thanks to its novel design, GECAM has accurately detected some important events, including the extremely bright GRBs (GRB 221009A and GRB 230307A) and mangetar bursts associated with (fast) radio bursts. In this talk, I will give an overview of GECAM mission, novel technologyies, and scientific achievements. I will also introduce the new instrument of GECAM which is under development.

Items.Authors: Carla J. Baldovin Saveedra, Bernard Asabere, Cees Bassa, Marchel Gerbers, Boudewijn Hut, Henri Meulman, David McKenna, Menno Norden, Sander ter Veen
Items.Title: LOFAR2.0 upgrade: AIV status update
Items.Abstract: LOFAR2.0 is a program of upgrades that will improve every aspect of the LOFAR telescope. Different teams work on specific sub-systems with different timelines and their own challenges, but at the end everything needs to come together.     The upgrade of the LOFAR stations is executed by the Assembly Integration and Verification (AIV) team. The activities include decommissioning of LOFAR, integration and testing of the LOFAR2.0 hardware, installation in the stations, testing and verification. Several teams work in parallel to deliver LOFAR2.0 stations for commissioning.     AIV activities started in full swing in January 2025 and will continue throughout 2026 to upgrade all stations in EU. I will describe the project management perspective, provide a status update of AIV activities; sharing the main challenges and lessons, and put in context the LOFAR2.0 AIV phase with respect to other facilities.

Items.Authors: Alain C. Carrier, Kiarash Tajdaran, Michael Jacoby, Alison Nordt, Liz Osborne, Jacob Wirth, Rodrigo Zeledon
Items.Title: Progress on large ultra-stable space observatory architectures for direct exo-earth planet imaging
Items.Abstract: We report on our evaluation of the end-to-end dynamic stability performance achieved on a pathfinder observatory architecture developed by NASA and its partners called EAC1. The optical telescope assembly consists of an off-axis 6-meter inscribed-diameter segmented primary mirror with 19 segments and an unobscured telescope. Our reporting covers a layered control approach to achieving the requisite wavefront stability combining Lockheed Martin’s Disturbance Free Payload (DFP) system for vibration isolation from the host spacecraft to the telescope, and active wavefront sensing and control of the primary mirror segment and the secondary mirror complete with picometer-class metrology and actuation. DFP enables high science observation efficiencies with little-to-no downtime following slews and tight telescope precision pointing control at ~0.6-Hz bandwidth. We discuss the implications for the design of the observatory and its active wavefront sensing and control system.

Items.Authors: Michael D. Johnson, Kazunori Akiyama, Rebecca Baturin, Peter Galison, Janice Houston, Sara Issaoun, Alexandru Lupsasca, Daniel P. Marrone
Items.Title: The Black Hole Explorer
Items.Abstract: The Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) will be the first submillimeter Earth–space very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) mission, delivering the sharpest images in the history of astronomy. BHEX will measure fundamental properties of supermassive black holes and their relativistic jets, enabling transformational discoveries that directly address key priorities of the Astro2020 Decadal Survey. In particular, BHEX will measure the sharp “photon ring” that is predicted to exist in images of black holes from light that orbited the black hole before escaping. In addition to detailed studies of the nearby supermassive black holes M87* and Sgr A*, BHEX will probe the growth of supermassive black holes by measuring apparent shadow sizes for a broad population of targets. Here, we present the science objectives and recent technical developments of BHEX, which is being developed for launch within the next decade as a NASA Small Explorer (SMEX) mission.

Items.Authors: Dimitra Rigopoulou, Peter R. Roelfsema, William Grainger, Chris Pearson, Boon-Kok Tan, Wouter Laauwen, Andrey Baryshev, Vincent Desmaris, Ismael G. Bernete, Javier Goicoechea, Giorgios Magdis, Miguel Pereira, Kamber Schwarz, Martina Wiedner
Items.Title: The Line Emission TeraHertz Observatory: exploring the lifecycle of the ISM and the origins of water
Items.Abstract: The Line Emission Terahertz Observatory (LETO) is designed to unravel the interrelation between stars and The InterStellar Medium (ISM) in much more detail than was possible ever before, by providing capabilities required to obtain extremely sensitive and high resolution spectroscopic measurements in key Far-Infrared (FIR) molecular and atomic transitions. The ISM is the reservoir of baryonic matter from which stars and planetary systems are formed. Also it is the repository of the material that is expelled at the end of the stellar evolutionary cycle feeding the baryonic matter reservoir. These evolutionary phases in the ISM together form a complex interplay driving planet and star formation and thus the evolution of our own Milky Way as well as galaxies at low and high redshifts. In this paper we will describe the science drivers of the LETO mission as well as the mission concept.

Items.Authors: Armando Gil de Paz, Patricia Sánchez-Blázquez, Jesús Gallego, Esperanza Carrasco, Marisa García Vargas, Javier Piqueras López, José Oñorbe, Gracia Esther Martín Garzón, Sergio Pascual, Nicolás Cardiel, África Castillo-Morales, Francisco M. Montenegro Montes
Items.Title: TARSIS, an 8 arcmin^2 IFU under detailed design for the Calar Alto 3.5m telescope
Items.Abstract: TARSIS (Tetra-Armed Super-Ifu Spectrograph) is a wide-field IFU with an 8-arcmin^2 FoV that is currently under detailed design for the Calar Alto Observatory (CAHA) 3.5m telescope. The TARSIS image-slicer fills the instrument FoV completely and, combined with the TARSIS four spectrographs, yields a spectral resolution of R~1000 in the range between 320-520nm (three spectrographs/quadrants) and 510-810nm (one spectrograph/quadrant) with a spaxel size of 2x2 arcsec^2. The scientific objective of TARSIS is to carry out the CATARSIS survey, a blind-spectroscopic mapping of 16 galaxy clusters in the range 0.15< z<0.27 up to their virial radii that will make use of all available dark time at the CAHA 3.5m for five years. CATARSIS will start as soon as TARSIS is available at the telescope, which is estimated for 2030.

Items.Authors: Thomas Granzer, Michael Weber, Jörg Weingrill, Klaus G. Strassmeier
Items.Title: 20 years of continuous robotic observation: The two STELLA telescopes
Items.Abstract: The STELLA robotic observatory consists of two 1.2m alt-az telescopes, which were built by   Halfmann Telescopes in the early 2000s. It is located at the Izana Observatory at the Canary Islands.   It combines high-resolution echelle spectroscopy (R=55,000) on STELLA-2 with a wide   field-of-view photometry (FoV 22 arcmin) on STELLA-1.  The first data were collected in fully robotic mode in 2006;   operations have been ongoing uninterrupted for twenty years now. The primary design goal   of the robotic software -- flexibility and reusability -- allowed seamless integration of   new instruments.   The primary pipelines provides science-ready data within one day.   In this talk, I will provide an overview of the system, spend some time on lessons learnt and   will introduce the two new instruments that are due in 2026/27:   a low read-noise sCMOS camera and a vacuum-stabilized three-arm spectrograph.

Items.Authors: Jackson Zariski, Kaitlin Kratter, Chad Bender, Mark Bowman
Items.Title: A machine learning pipeline for real-time telescope offset correction
Items.Abstract: Modern telescope networks collect large amounts of data, but acquisition still often depends on static pointing models and manual tweaking. We present a data-driven, machine-learning pipeline to automatically predict and correct acquisition offsets, demonstrated on archival logs from the Las Cumbres Observatory network. Our approach uses both traditional and deep-learning based regression models to learn how offsets depend on observing and instrumentation conditions, and a sensitivity analysis step to guide automated model tuning. We also test our methods on controlled synthetic data to understand the best accuracy a chosen model architecture could reasonably achieve and present a novel technique for performance analysis based on spike-peeling and probabilistic combinatorics. Finally, we present our open-source Dockerized service with a browser-based GUI for easy, real-time use by observatory staff.

Items.Authors: Oriol Casamor, Manuel Canchado, Miguel Redondo, Albert Tomàs, Joan Manel Casalta, Patrick Caillier, Lluis Cavaller, Martin Dimmler
Items.Title: High-Precision Remote Handling for the ELT: Design and Verification of the Segment Manipulator
Items.Abstract: The ELT Segment Manipulator is a fully automated remote-handling system designed to install and exchange the 798 primary mirror segments of the ELT. Its core is a lightweight cable-actuated hexapod that has been verified to achieve large motion ranges with millimetric and milliradian accuracy, supported by a 23-m hoist system and a multilayer sensing and vision architecture for safe alignment. This contribution summarizes the main engineering challenges and presents verification results demonstrating compliance with the demanding operational, seismic, and safety requirements of the observatory.

Items.Authors: Angel C. Otarola, Ivo Saviane, Andres González, Edison Bustos, Andrei Tokovinin, José Figueroa, Francisco Olivares, Steffen Mieske
Items.Title: RINGSS turbulence profiler at ESO’s La Silla observatory: one year+ of operations
Items.Abstract: Monitoring atmospheric turbulence at an astronomical observatory is a key aspect of science operations. The information on atmospheric turbulence plays avital role in making informed decisions in the sequence of astronomical objects to be observed (in visitor mode). As well as, for the filtering and ranking of the observing block queue (in service mode of science operations).     In this work we will present information on the development, installation, and operation of the first Rings New Generation Scintillation Sensor (RINGSS) at the European Southern Observatory’s La Silla Observatory. This instrument enables science operations with timely information on the total atmospheric seeing, free-atmosphere seeing, coherence time of the turbulence, isoplanatic angle, and ground-layer turbulence fraction.

Items.Authors: Tyler M. McCracken, Laura Coyle, Benjamin Cromey, Joseph Ho, Thomas Peters, Daniel Porpora, Jeremy Shugrue, James Tersigni, Sebastian Valencia
Items.Title: Advancements in rigid body sensing and control for large, ultra-stable segmented apertures
Items.Abstract: BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems has led a series of NASA-funded programs under the Ultra-stable Large Telescope Research and Analysis (ULTRA) umbrella performing research and development of key technologies for NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). One of the highest priority technology gaps for the HWO architecture is limiting the rigid body motion of the telescope optics to achieve the demanding wavefront stability needed by the coronagraph. Thus, a major focus of the current ULTRA program is building a subscale, three segment testbed to demonstrate segment level sensing and control to technology readiness level 4/5 at the fidelity needed for HWO. This paper will discuss component technologies, specifically picometer capable actuators and capacitive sensors, and the status of the multiple-segment testbed that is currently in assembly at BAE Systems SMS in preparation for testing at the Goddard Ultrastable Laboratory in the summer of 2026.

Items.Authors: Yuh-Jing Hwang, Bangwon Lee, MingJye Wang, Yu Chieh Huang, Chau-Ching Chiong, Yue-Fang Kuo, Cheuk-Yu Edward Tong, Yan-Jun Wang, Chen Chien, Chin-Ting Ho, Tse-Jun Chen, Wei-Chun Lu, Yen-Pin Chang, Hsiao-Wen Chang, Keng-Yu Yeh, Chuang-Ping Chiu, Jia-Ruei Nian, Fang-Yu Hsu, Pai-An Chen, Lou-Chien Lu, Patrick Koch
Items.Title: Band-4+5 initial prototype receiver front-end for ALMA2030 wideband sensitivity upgrade
Items.Abstract: The ALMA Band-4+5 receivers are proposed for the upgrade after 2030. The new receiver will cover the RF frequency of the original Band-4 and Band-5 to reach 125 -211 GHz continuous frequency tuning over dual polarizations, dual sidebands with instantaneous intermediate frequency (IF) bandwidth up to 16 GHz per sideband and per polarization.    The SIS-based receiver scheme is chosen as the baseline design. The development of the key components, and the performance of the key components and the receiver cartridge will be presented. The key components with 51.2% relative bandwidth developed in-house are (i) Nb SIS mixers, (ii) 3-dB waveguide hybrid couplers, (iii) orthomode transducers, (iv) corrugated horn antenna, (v) optics mirror pairs.

Items.Authors: David Sweeney, Stephanie Rossini-Bryson, Peter Tuthill, Barnaby Norris, Olivier Guyon
Items.Title: Beyond numerical self-calibration: a machine-learning framework for photonic nulling data
Items.Abstract: Photonic nulling interferometers such as GLINT promise extreme starlight suppression for characterizing habitable exoplanet atmospheres, but their performance is limited by imperfect calibration of instrumental and atmospheric noise. Existing approaches like numerical self-calibration (NSC) treat each frame independently and degrade in the low noise regime. We present a machine-learning analysis that learns the photonic chip response from the data while modelling the temporal evolution of the atmosphere induced phase delay with physically motivated priors. Using simulations and laboratory measurements representative of GLINT we compare the recovery of astrophysical null depth to NSC and examine maximum achievable performance.

Items.Authors: Takayuki J. Hayashi, Rozenn Boissay-Malaquin, Keisuke Tamura, Takashi Okajima, Eric Miller, Aurora Simionescu, Matteo Guainazzi, Toshiki Sato, Tahir Yaqoob, Arnab Sarkar, Aysegul Tumer, Maxim Markevitch
Items.Title: In-flight measurements of the optical axis and stray light of x-ray mirror assembly (XMA) on XRISM
Items.Abstract: The X-ray astronomy satellite XRISM, which was launched in 2023, carries two complementary instruments: Resolve and Xtend. Resolve has a high energy resolution (~5 eV at 6 keV) in a 3'x3' FoV. Xtend offers a wide FoV (38'x38') with a moderate energy resolution (~180 eV at 6 keV). Both instruments are equipped with almost identical mirrors, called the X-ray Mirror Assembly (XMA).The in-flight optical axis of Xtend was well-measured with off-axis observations of A2029 with its large FoV. In this measurement, the asymmetric vignetting, which was created by the XMA segment boundaries, was taken into consideration. By contrast, the optical axis measurement of Resolve is difficult due to its small FoV, and no such observation has been carried out. The in-flight stray patterns were clearly observed by Xtend with Crab at 60' off-axis. Based on the spectrum taken by Xtend, a simulation shows that the stray light of Resolve is no stronger than the NXB as long as the gate valve is closed.

Items.Authors: Tobias Glaubach, Oliver Polch, Yanik Yiannakis, Gundolf Wieching
Items.Title: Scalable verification: a generalized test execution system for verification during mid-volume production of astronomy instrumentation
Items.Abstract: As radio astronomy shifts from single telescopes to large arrays, traditional manual verification methods fail to scale, yet rigid industrial quality assurance processes lack the flexibility required for the manufacturing of scientific instruments. This paper introduces a novel, open-source software solution designed to bridge this gap for mid-scale production (10–1000 units).    The tool enables flexible production testing and commissioning while ensuring rigorous traceability, reproducibility, and centralized data management. Its effectiveness was demonstrated through the verification of the MeerKAT Band 5b receiver and its sub-assemblies. The study concludes by discussing the software's performance, lessons learned, and future development.

Items.Authors: Gábor D. Furesz, Rob Simcoe, Elio Angile, Gerardo Berlanga Molina, Mark Egan, Michelle Gabutti, Jozsef Lazar, Andrew Malonis, Rebecca Mastersson, Blake Mitchell, Cody Schneller, Joshua Brwon, Chris Buttaccio, Kristin Clark, Danielle Frostig, Erik Hinrichsen, Christopher Hunt, Jill Juneau, Nathan Lourie, Sean MacBride, Micheal McDonald, Ace Metivier, Gustav Pettersson, Jack Piotrowski, Gabe Raiber, Thomas Savatovsky, Corrie Smeaton, June Stenzel
Items.Title: First year into operations of LLAMAS, the Large Lenslet Array Magellan spectrograph: design, build and commissioning overview, results and performance, lessons learned
Items.Abstract: LLAMAS, The Large Lenslet Array MAgellan Spectrograph is a (largely) NSF-funded facility Integral Field Unit (IFU) spectrograph commissioned late 2024 at the Las Campanas Observatory on one of the (Baade) 6.5-meter Magellan Telescopes. It covers a 35x35 arcsec solid angle with 2,392 optical fibers efficiently coupled by a double-sided microlens-array, producing R=2,000 spectra with 0.75arcsec spatial resolution. Its broad passband (340-1000nm) offers access to line and continuum measurements over a wide range in redshift. The short fiber run (3m) from the IFU feeds 8 compact, carbon-fiber bench mounted spectrographs utilizing VPH grisms and passband optimized three arms within each. We employed several trades on cost/performance while optimizing LLAMAS' system design, and mitigated technical risks through extensive prototyping. Despite challenges posed by the pandemic and some late-realized risks, we delivered the instrument under 6 years and on a $9M budget, using a very small team.

Items.Authors: Axel Yanes-Díaz, Sergio Rueda Teruel, Fernando Rueda Teruel, Antonio Marín Franch, Rafael Bello, Jorge Ventura-Guillamón, Mikel Domínguez-Martínez, Nuria Martínez-Olivar, Juan Manuel Olivas-Galve, Guillermo López-Alegre, Sergio Chueca, Luis Alberto Rodríguez-García, Raúl Domínguez, Héctor de Paz, Manuel Huertas, César Iñiguez, Tamara Civera, José Javier Collado-Escusa, María Rosario Mayoral-Blasco, Jordi Albero-Gamir, David Garcés-Cubel, Said Farah-Amin, María Almarcegui-Gracia, A. Javier Cenarro, Romano Corradi, Mariano Moles, Carlos López-Sanjuan, Héctor Vázquez-Ramió, Javier Zaragoza-Cardiel, Luisa Valdivielso-Casas, Javier Lizaga-Villarroya, Stelios Pyrzas, Miguel Chioare Díaz-Martín, Ramón Iglesias-Marzoa, Clara Cabanillas-de-la-Casa, Natalio Maícas-Sacristán, José Luis Lamadrid-Gutiérrez, Fátima López-Martínez, Francisco José Galindo-Guil, Elvis Lacruz-Calderón, Juan Castillo, Ángel López-Sainz, Mohammad Akhlaghi, Javier Hernández-Fuertes, David José Muniesa-Gallardo, Alberto Moreno-Signes, Antonio Hernán-Caballero, Giacomo Lorenzetti, Alessandro Ederoclite, Juan Antonio Fernández-Ontiveros, Raúl Infante-Sainz, Sepideh Eskandarlou, David Fernández-Gil, Adrián Hidalgo-Pinilla, David Morate-González, Nischal Acharya, Borja Anguiano, Karla Ziboney Arellano-Cordova, Sayali Kulkarni, David Martínez-Delgado, Bojan Novakovic, Francisco Javier Sáez-Ruiz, Stefano Zarattini, Silvia Vaquero-Valer, Inés Muñoz-Igado, María Teresa Alegre-Sánchez, Gema María Julián-Caballero-de-España, Rosa Allueva-Gómez, Ana López-Colás
Items.Title: Artificial Intelligence for OAJ Observatory Operations: From Concept to Practice with OPTIMIA, a Multi-Agent AI Operational Brain
Items.Abstract: Building on our previous work on the preliminary AI design for operations at the OAJ, presented at the last meeting, we report on the deployment of OPTIMIA, an AI-driven “operational brain” for the observatory. OPTIMIA is a multi-agent AI system integrated with the Observatory Control System (GOCS) and operational tools, providing AI-assisted support across all GOCS operation types. Using on-premises large language models and retrieval-augmented generation over telemetry, alarms, maintenance records, logs and procedures, OPTIMIA offers conversational and voice interfaces that help staff diagnose faults, prioritise incidents and execute complex procedures. Exploiting its ability to connect large volumes of heterogeneous data, OPTIMIA becomes a powerful guide for orientation, coordination and management. We also outline the risks and challenges of being early adopters of this technology and how careful planning is essential to gain benefits without compromising safety or reliability.

Items.Authors: Kazunori Akiyama, Mareki Honma, Akihiro Doi, Shoko Koyama, Kotaro Niinuma, Kazuhiro Hada, Yuto Akiyama, Rebecca Baturin, Peter Galison, Yoshiaki Hagiwara, Aya E. Higuchi, Janice Houston, Michael D. Johnson, Tomohisa Kawashima, Daniel P. Marrone, Yosuke Murayama, Ryo Saito, Ken Ohsuga, Hannah Rana, Hidetoshi Sano, Edward Tong, Yuh Tsunetoe, Yoshinori Uzawa
Items.Title: Black Hole Explorer mission development in Japan
Items.Abstract: The Black Hole Explorer (BHEX) is a next-generation space very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) mission concept that will extend the ground-based Black Hole Telescope into space. Japan plays a central role in the mission development through the BHEX Japan Consortium, ranging from science requirement studies to mission-critical instrumentation. In June 2025, the BHEX Working Group was established under the JAXA Space Science Committee for Pre-Phase A mission development, including cryocooling system design, development of the BHEX SIS mixer, and studies of science requirements. This talk will outline progress on the BHEX mission development in Japan, from science drivers to instrument design.

Items.Authors: Jonathan Kadan, Justin Fletcher, Cameron Harris, Connor Segal
Items.Title: MACHINA: sensor orchestration for time dominant space situational awareness
Items.Abstract: Safe space vehicle operation is predicated upon transparent and responsive sensor orchestration in support of Space Traffic Management (STM). Recent work introduced the MACHINA agent framework in support of this objective, and has demonstrated live, open-loop space vehicle tracking objective execution. By advancing from open-loop scheduling to a validated, closed-loop agent, MACHINA provides a scalable software architecture for ensuring the long-term sustainability of space. The MACHINA-sim environment offers a powerful capability for verifying MACHINA's autonomous sensor orchestration systems meets the collaborative and dynamic demands of modern space operations.

Items.Authors: Kathryn Hartley, Timothy Morris, Timothy Butterley, Jurgen Schmoll, Emily Ronson, David Barr, John Connolly, Thomas Davies, Dirk Schmidt, Luke Johnson
Items.Title: Nēnē: a solar-SLODAR turbulence profiler on the DKIST Telescope
Items.Abstract: Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics (MCAO) is a critical step toward achieving high-resolution, wide-field solar observations, including detailed studies of sunspots and active solar regions. Effective MCAO tomography requires accurate knowledge of the vertical atmospheric turbulence profile. To address this need, we present the preliminary results of Nēnē, a solar-SLODAR optical turbulence profiler installed on the 4 m DKIST Telescope in Maui, Hawai’i. The instrument uses an adaptation of the SLODAR turbulence profiling technique that uses granulation on the solar surface as a reference to measure differential tip/tilt across the telescope pupil. The instrument design, real time control and data reduction pipeline will be presented along with preliminary on-sun turbulence profile measurements.

Items.Authors: Keath Beifus, William Burgett, Colby Gottschalk, King-Ming Lam, Sam Park, Nathan Loewen, Byron Smith, Giovanni Bonomi, Jeff Kimberly, Todd Trieloff, Dave Zarembski, Peter Eisenträger, Volker Grimm, Alexei Ippa, Alexander Rohr, Lehel Simeny, Eberhard Sust, Ulrich Weis, Raffaele Tomelleri
Items.Title: The Giant Magellan Telescope azimuth track: fabrication and machining processes
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) Azimuth Track forms a 20 m diameter, multi-segmented cylinder that supports three concentric hydrostatic bearing raceways requiring 250-micron flatness across the entire diameter. Eight identical segments, each averaging 27,200 kg, are fabricated from A572 Gr50 plate ranging from 25–100 mm in thickness. High-density finite element analysis (FEA) drove the inclusion of numerous large complete joint penetration (CJP) welds, with thermal stress relief cycles applied to mitigate distortion. After welding, segments are rough-machined for precise geometry; axial raceways are finished by milling, and radial raceways by single-point turning and abrasive machining. Integrated features manage hydrostatic bearing oil flow and collection.

Items.Authors: Akio Taniguchi, Yoichi Tamura, Takeshi Sakai, Masato Hagimoto, Takuya Hashimoto, Akio K. Inoue, Shun Ishii, Haoran Kang, Masato Kato, Ryohei Kawabe, Kotaro Kohno, Takafumi Kojima, Kianhong Lee, Sho Masui, Akinobu Miyake, Taku Nakajima, Tai Oshima, Wenlei Shan, Tatsuya Takekoshi, Kunihiko Tanaka, Kotomi Taniguchi, Kaoru Tsuji, Issei Watanabe, Tom J. L. C. Bakx, Yoshinobu Fudamoto, Kazuyuki Fujita, Yuichi Harikane, Bunyo Hatsukade, David H. Hughes, Takahiro Iino, Yuki Kimura, Hiroyuki Maezawa, Yuichi Matsuda, Ken Mawatari, Shunichi Nakatsubo, Hideo Sagawa, Peter F. Schloerb, Shigeru Takahashi, Akiyoshi Tsujita, Hideki Umehata, Min S. Yun
Items.Title: FINER: development of the wideband millimeter-wave receiver system and preparations for first light on the Large Millimeter Telescope
Items.Abstract: The recent discovery of an excess of luminous galaxies in the early Universe necessitates sensitive and wideband millimeter spectroscopy to understand their rapid growth. To address this, we present the development of the Far-Infrared Nebular Emission Receiver (FINER) for the Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT). The FINER frontend comprises two receivers covering 120–350 GHz (corresponding to ALMA Bands 4+5 and 6+7). The warm optics are designed to enable simultaneous two-band observations. Combined with the 10.24-GHz-wide digital spectrometer array, the system aims to deliver an instantaneous bandwidth approximately five times wider than current ALMA capabilities. We report that the 210-350 GHz receiver has already achieved commissioning-level performance, with sideband rejection further enhanced by the digital sideband separation technique. With installation expected in 2026, we discuss parallel preparations, including integrated testing and commissioning plans for first-look targets.

Items.Authors: Sarah Pappert, Guillaume Bourdarot, Richard Davies, Frank Eisenhauer, Helmut Feuchtgruber, Simon Flesch, Natascha Förster Schreiber, Quentin Fournier, Reinhard Genzel, Stefan Gillessen, Simran Joharle, Ruancun Li, Dieter Lutz, Felix Mang, Thomas Ott, Sebastian Rabien, Diogo Ribeiro, Matteo Sadun Bordoni, Jinyi Shangguan, Taro T. Shimizu, Eckhard Sturm, Linda Tacconi
Items.Title: GRAVITY+ at the VLTI: instrumental advances enabling high-angular-resolution AGN science
Items.Abstract: We present an overview of how recent and upcoming GRAVITY+ upgrades at the VLTI interconnect instrument and science, enabling high-angular-resolution studies of active galactic nuclei (AGN). Improvements such as wide-angle off-axis fringe tracking, enhanced fringe-tracker performance, and state-of-the-art adaptive optics, including laser guide stars, increase sensitivity and sky coverage, allowing coherent observations of fainter targets. These instrumental advances directly support measurements of black hole masses out to high redhsift and spatially resolved studies of broad-line region structure and kinematics, as well as resolved observations of [O III] emission tracing the inner narrow-line region at z ≈ 2–4. We also discuss prospects for supermassive black hole binary searches with GRAVITY+.
